newsitem.title: USA: Senators introduce bill to reform U.S. futures law.
newsitem.headline: Senators introduce bill to reform U.S. futures law.

text.p: Senators Richard Lugar and Patrick Leahy introduced a bill on Monday to reform the Commodity Exchange Act, the primary U.S. law governing futures trading.

Lugar, chairman of the Senate Agriculture Committee, and Leahy, the ranking minority member, conceded that the bill had no chance of passing in the current Congressional session. But the senators said the bill would provide a starting point for reforming the act next year.
The current law "works well but we can modify it to reduce some unnecessary regulation and make it clearer," Lugar said.

The bill includes some changes requested by U.S. futures exchanges, a provision to address issues raised by the Sumitomo Corp copper scandal, and an attempt to bring greater legal certainty to the over-the-counter derivatives market.
Officials at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, charged with enforcing the Commodity Exchange Act, had no comment on Monday on the proposals.
In the past, CFTC officials have said there is little need to amend existing futures regulations.
Newly sworn-in CFTC chairwoman Brooksley Born reiterated that position in a recent letter to the Senate Agriculture Committee, CFTC and Senate staffers said.
The bill by Lugar, an Indiana Republican, and Leahy, a Vermont Democrat, would allow the exchanges to begin trading in new futures contracts far more quickly than under current law.
Under current law, a new contract is presumed unacceptable until the CFTC gives its approval, usually in about 90 days.
The bill would reverse that presumption, allowing trading to begin in 10 days unless the CFTC registers an objection, a Senate staffer said.
The bill would also give the CFTC new jurisdiction over foreign futures contracts on which delivery can be made in the United States.
Sumitomo Corp, which lost $1.8 billion through allegedly unauthorized copper trading over 10 years, did almost no trading at U.S. exchanges, instead using the less-regulated London Metal Exchange.
But the CFTC is investigating the Japanese commodity giant to see if it enagaged in a scheme to manipulate world copper prices, in part by delivering copper to an LME warehouse in California.

The bill directs the CFTC to consult with overseas regulators and other parties where futures exchanges have established U.S. delivery points. The bill also requires that the warehouses collect and make available to the CFTC useful information such as trades and positions.
For over-the-counter swaps, the bill would enact into law a 1993 regulation adopted by the CFTC that exempts such instruments from most futures regulation.
That would prevent the CFTC from revoking the 1993 exemption on its own, an unlikely possibility that has nonetheless troubled swap market participants.

The bill asks the CFTC to study its deployment of enforcement resources and report back to Congress in one year. Some market participants feel the CFTC is spending too much time and money on enforcement actions that could be handled by the exchanges or by industry groups.

The bill would also require the CFTC to weigh the costs as well as the benefits of new regulations under consideration and free the exchanges from a requirement to deploy high-tech trade-auditing systems.
